title: Gravity Echoes from Supermassive Black Hole Binaries
summary: Pulsar timing arrays record gravitational waves from supermassive black hole binaries at two spacetime points: an Earth term, measured when the wave passes the Earth, and a pulsar term, measured when the wave passed each pulsar at an earlier epoch. We show that a future $μ$Hz-band detection of a nearby massive binary by a mission such as $μ$Ares would turn PTA pulsar terms into targeted probes of binary evolution. In analogy with supernova light echoes, each pulsar term acts as a gravity echo: a dated snapshot of the binary at an earlier stage of its inspiral. Together, the $μ$Hz Earth-term measurement and the nHz pulsar-term echoes provide a temporal baseline that neither detector could access alone. For a fiducial equal-mass binary with total mass $10^9\,M_\odot$ at 80~Mpc, we find a combined pulsar timing array echo signal-to-noise ratio of 33, with up to 24 pulsars individually resolving the signal among pulsars with 50-year baselines. The angular dependence of the single-pulsar echo sensitivity alone enables independent sky localization of the source to $\sim$10--100~deg$^2$, and the resolved pulsar-term frequencies directly measure the binary inspiral rate hundreds to thousands of years ago. With sufficient pulsar distance precision, a small set of anchor pulsars could additionally phase-connect the array and trace the post-Newtonian evolution coherently over kpc baselines. The source population required for gravity echoes is drawn from the same massive-end census responsible for the observed nanoHertz stochastic background.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes leveraging future μHz-band gravitational wave detectors like μAres alongside pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) to use pulsar timing signals as 'gravity echoes,' capturing historical snapshots of supermassive black hole binaries' inspiral stages. This combination enhances temporal baseline and source localization, allowing precise binary evolution studies over centuries to millennia.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limitation of single-point gravitational wave observations from PTAs and enable direct temporal tracking of the inspiral history of supermassive black hole binaries, thereby enhancing our understanding of binary evolution across long timescales.
AI.method: The study models gravitational wave signals from massive equal-mass binaries and simulates combined observations by μHz-band detectors and PTA pulsar timing signals, analyzing signal-to-noise ratios, angular sensitivity, and the potential for phase-connecting pulsars based on distance precision to extract evolutionary dynamics coherently.
AI.result: A combined PTA echo signal-to-noise ratio of 33 is achievable for a typical massive binary at 80 Mpc, with up to 24 pulsars able to individually resolve signals over 50 years, enabling source localization within 10–100 deg² and direct measurements of inspiral rates centuries to millennia ago.
AI.conclusion: Combining μHz Earth-term gravitational wave measurements with nHz pulsar-term echoes enables targeted, historical probes of supermassive black hole binary evolution, improving signal-to-noise, source localization to tens of square degrees, and measurement of inspiral rates long before detection capabilities of individual detectors.

title: Archival Multiband Gravitational-Wave Signals from Massive Black Hole Binary Mergers
summary: While massive black hole binaries (MBHBs) merge at gravitational-wave frequencies above the pulsar timing array (PTA) sensitivity band, we show that they leave orphaned low-frequency contributions in the PTA pulsar term. Due to the light-propagation time between each pulsar in the array and Earth, the pulsar term acts as a time-delayed probe of a chirping merger with a specific frequency response determined by the direction of origin and intrinsic properties of the MBHB. We provide a detailed consideration of how such a multiband signal would manifest in a full PTA, demonstrate an approach to stack these orphaned pulsar terms across the array, and discuss prospects for an archival, multiband search in conjunction with MBHB mergers observed in astrometric data or spaceborne interferometers like LISA.

AI.tldr: This study reveals that low-frequency signatures of massive black hole binary mergers, undetectable directly by pulsar timing arrays, can be traced in the pulsar term across the array. By stacking these signals, it is possible to perform multiband gravitational-wave searches that complement LISA and astrometric data, improving prospects for detecting and characterizing MBHB mergers.
AI.motivation: To detect gravitational wave signals from massive black hole binaries that merge at frequencies beyond current pulsar timing array sensitivity, by exploiting low-frequency contributions in the pulsar term as a complementary probe.
AI.method: Detailed analysis of the pulsar term's time-delayed frequency response due to light-travel time to pulsars, development of a stacking approach to combine signals across the pulsar timing array, and investigation of how these multiband signals appear in full PTA observations.
AI.result: Identification of orphaned low-frequency gravitational-wave contributions in the pulsar term linked to MBHB mergers, demonstration of stacking methods to enhance detection, and outlining the feasibility of archival multiband searches in conjunction with spaceborne interferometric and astrometric observations.
AI.conclusion: Orphaned low-frequency signals in the pulsar term act as a valuable, time-delayed probe of MBHB mergers beyond the PTA band, enabling complementary multiband gravitational-wave observations and enhanced detection prospects through combined PTA and external data sources.

title: An Analytic Threshold for LESA-Driven Negative ELN Flux Directions in Core-Collapse Supernovae: Derivation and Population Census
summary: In core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe), deleptonization normally favors $ν_e$ over $\barν_e$ emission. However, lepton-number emission self-sustained asymmetry (LESA) can make the energy-integrated emitted lepton-number flux negative along some directions. We derive a simple diagnostic for this transition and test it in 33 independent 3D CCSN simulations: 25 Princeton/Fornax models ($8.1$--$100\,M_\odot$) and 8 Garching models, including non-, slow-, and fast-rotating $15\,M_\odot$ cases. Of 23 non-black-hole-forming Princeton models, 22 cross the threshold, with median onset $t_c=225\,\mathrm{ms}$, IQR $162$--$264\,\mathrm{ms}$, and cross-model scatter $\mathrm{CV}=18.6\%$. Full-sky flux-sign searches show that the threshold identifies the anti-LESA-pole transition, distinguishing the global LESA-driven crossing from early localized turbulent crossings. The fast-rotating Garching $15\,M_\odot$ model, where rapid rotation suppresses the LESA dipole, is correctly classified as a non-crosser without using any rotation parameter. Both black-hole-forming Princeton models cross near $250\,\mathrm{ms}$ post-bounce and remain above threshold for $1807$ and $2463\,\mathrm{ms}$ before collapse. Thus, in the next nearby CCSN, the emitted $\barν_e$ energy flux may exceed the $ν_e$ flux along some lines of sight. Such directions may also correlate with sustained fast flavor instability, although testing this requires local phase-space distributions or dedicated linear stability analysis. The relevant quantity here is the energy-integrated emitted flux field, i.e. a luminosity difference per steradian, not a neutrino number flux.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a diagnostic test for when LESA causes electron antineutrino emission to exceed electron neutrino emission in core-collapse supernovae, validating this across many 3D simulations and highlighting its implications for neutrino observables and flavor instability.
AI.motivation: To understand the conditions and characteristics under which LESA causes the lepton-number flux to become negative in certain directions during core-collapse supernovae, challenging the typical dominance of electron neutrino emission over electron antineutrino emission.
AI.method: Derivation of a simple diagnostic criterion for the transition in the lepton-number emission flux sign and its testing across 33 independent 3D CCSN simulations, including Princeton/Fornax and Garching models with various progenitor masses and rotation speeds.
AI.result: The diagnostic effectively identifies the transition threshold in most non-black-hole-forming CCSN models, showing median onset around 225 ms post-bounce, distinguishing global LESA-driven emission asymmetry from early localized turbulence, and correctly classifying non-crossing fast-rotating models. Black-hole-forming models also cross the threshold and persist above it before collapse.
AI.conclusion: The energy-integrated emitted lepton-number flux can become negative in specific directions during CCSNe due to LESA, influencing neutrino flux observations and possibly correlating with flavor instabilities; the introduced diagnostic reliably identifies this transition across diverse simulation models.

title: Interpretable Analytic Formulae for GWTC-4 Binary Black Hole Population Properties via Symbolic Regression
summary: Recent LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) analyses have revealed complex structure in the binary black hole (BBH) population, including distinct features in the primary mass spectrum and nontrivial spin-mass correlations. However, the phenomenological models used to capture these features often lack analytic transparency, making it difficult to isolate robust physical laws from modeling artifacts. To address this, symbolic regression is applied to the posterior inference products of the GWTC-4 catalog, discovering compact, closed-form analytic expressions for four key population relationships: (i) the merger-rate evolution with redshift; (ii) the mass-ratio dependence of the effective-spin distribution; (iii) the redshift evolution of the effective-spin distribution; and (iv) the conditional mass-ratio distributions associated with the 10 solar mass and 35 solar mass primary mass peaks. This framework successfully compresses both rigid and highly flexible models into differentiable phenomenological laws, dynamically recovering a consistent low-redshift merger-rate slope without assuming an a priori power-law form. The exact analytic derivatives provided by symbolic regression show that the mass ratio--effective spin and redshift--effective spin correlations are robustly driven by broadening of the posterior widths rather than shifts in the mean. Furthermore, qualitatively distinct functional forms for the mass-ratio distributions conditioned on the 10 solar mass and 35 solar mass primary mass peaks are identified. These closed-form expressions enable exact analytic gradient diagnostics and compact surrogate summaries, particularly for flexible numerical posteriors that are not otherwise available in low-dimensional analytic form. They also facilitate rapid downstream calculations for rate forecasting, formation channel comparison, and stochastic background estimation.

AI.tldr: Symbolic regression extracted clear analytic laws from complex BBH population data, enabling precise diagnostics and rapid calculations for astrophysical applications.
AI.motivation: Existing phenomenological models of binary black hole populations lack analytic transparency, complicating the extraction of robust physical laws from modeling artifacts.
AI.method: Symbolic regression applied to posterior inference products of the GWTC-4 catalog
AI.result: Discovered compact, closed-form analytic expressions for four key population relationships related to merger-rate evolution, effective-spin distribution dependence on mass-ratio and redshift, and conditional mass-ratio distributions linked to primary mass peaks at 10 and 35 solar masses. The approach compressed complex models into differentiable phenomenological laws and identified robust correlations driven by posterior width broadening.
AI.conclusion: Closed-form analytic expressions derived via symbolic regression provide interpretable, differentiable models of BBH population features, supporting robust physical insights and efficient downstream astrophysical analyses.

title: Geometry, Not Calorimetry, Drives the Radio/Infrared/Gamma-Ray Correlation
summary: We investigate whether the observed radio-infrared-$γ$-ray correlation in star-forming galaxies is a geometric effect rather than a signature of local cosmic-ray (CR) calorimetry. Using the GALPROP framework, we generate synthetic observations for external viewers from a grid of 3D Milky Way models with varied CR source, gas, interstellar radiation, and magnetic field distributions, all normalised to reproduce local CR data. We find that a tight, quasi-linear correlation arises naturally from line-of-sight integration through the extended, radially-structured disc, even when local calorimetry is absent. The correlation's properties depend strongly on viewing geometry, preserving its form under moderate inclination but breaking down in edge-on views where galactic components are stratified. We conclude that the correlation is primarily an emergent property of geometric projection, not local physics. This implies that its scatter is likely not random noise but a diagnostic of underlying galactic structure and viewing angle.

AI.tldr: The observed radio-infrared-gamma-ray correlation in star-forming galaxies originates primarily from geometric projection effects through the galactic disc, challenging the interpretation as a direct signature of local cosmic-ray calorimetry.
AI.motivation: To determine if the known radio-infrared-gamma-ray correlation in star-forming galaxies is due to geometric projection effects rather than local cosmic-ray calorimetry processes.
AI.method: Using the GALPROP framework, synthetic observations are generated from a grid of 3D Milky Way models, varying cosmic ray (CR) sources, gas, interstellar radiation, and magnetic fields, normalized to local CR data.
AI.result: A tight, quasi-linear correlation arises naturally from line-of-sight integration through the galaxy disc without needing local calorimetry. The correlation's properties are sensitive to viewing geometry, maintaining form under moderate inclinations but breaking down when viewed edge-on.
AI.conclusion: The correlation between radio, infrared, and gamma-ray emissions is an emergent geometric effect of line-of-sight integration, not solely local cosmic-ray physics, and its scatter reveals information about galactic structure and viewing angles.

title: Relativistic effects in k-essence
summary: Relativistic effects are sensitive to subtle changes in dark energy. These effects grow on very large scales and at high redshifts, which will be the reach of upcoming surveys. We investigate these effects in both the linear and the angular galaxy power spectra in a late-time universe dominated by cold dark matter and k-essence, focusing on three core models (dilaton, tachyon, and DBI scalar fields) and contrasting their predictions with those of the concordance model. By enforcing identical present-day cosmological parameters, we isolate the imprints of k-essence dynamics and perturbations on very large scales. We found that relativistic corrections dominate on very large scales and grow with redshift, but are largely insensitive to k-essence microphysics in Fourier space, leading to strong degeneracies among the models. However, in the angular power spectrum, where line-of-sight integrals are naturally included, relativistic effects are significantly amplified, yielding better sensitivity to clustering k-essence. In particular, the tachyon exhibits clear deviations across multipoles and redshifts, with distinct imprints in the Doppler and the combined (velocity and gravitational) potentials contributions. Furthermore, our results show that neglecting relativistic corrections can lead to systematic misestimation of deviations of k-essence from the cosmological constant. Our results show the relativistic angular galaxy power spectrum as a more consistent and robust probe of ultra-large-scale physics. These findings underscore the need for full relativistic modelling in next-generation surveys that are targeting horizon-scale modes, where the imprint of non-standard dark energy is most pronounced.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how relativistic effects on large scales and high redshifts can reveal differences between standard cosmology and k-essence dark energy models, finding angular power spectra more sensitive than Fourier space. Neglecting relativistic corrections risks misestimating k-essence behaviors.
AI.motivation: To explore how relativistic effects on horizon scales can differentiate standard cosmology from k-essence dark energy models, especially as forthcoming surveys will probe very large scales and high redshifts where such effects grow and may reveal subtle dark energy dynamics.
AI.method: Analysis of relativistic effects on linear and angular galaxy power spectra at late times in a cold dark matter plus k-essence universe, comparing three scalar field models (dilaton, tachyon, DBI) against the concordance model by enforcing identical present-day cosmological parameters to isolate k-essence signatures.
AI.result: Relativistic corrections dominate on very large scales and grow with redshift but show strong degeneracies among models in Fourier space. In contrast, angular power spectra amplify relativistic effects and better distinguish k-essence clustering, notably the tachyon model, revealing distinct signatures. Neglecting relativistic corrections risks systematic misestimations of dark energy deviations.
AI.conclusion: Relativistic angular galaxy power spectra provide a robust probe of ultra-large-scale physics, exhibiting enhanced sensitivity to k-essence dark energy models compared to Fourier analyses, highlighting the necessity of full relativistic modeling in upcoming surveys to accurately capture non-standard dark energy signatures.

title: Bayesian Inference of Dense-Matter Equations of State from Small-Radius Compact Stars with Twin-Star Scenarios
summary: We investigate dense-matter equations of state (EOSs) within a Bayesian framework, with particular emphasis on whether recent small-radius compact-star candidates can be accommodated in a twin-star scenario. For the hadronic sector, we adopt a meta-modeling EOS constrained by the NICER mass--radius measurements of PSR J0030$+$0451, PSR J0437$-$4715, PSR J0614$-$3329, and the massive pulsar PSR J0740$+$6620. The hadronic inference indicates that PSR J0614$-$3329 favors a somewhat softer EOS than the other two \(\sim1.4\,M_\odot\) pulsars, while the \(\sim2\,M_\odot\) constraint prevents the EOS from becoming too soft. We then introduce a strong first-order phase transition through a constant-speed-of-sound quark-matter segment. Using HESS J1731$-$347 and XTE J1814$-$338 to constrain the phase-transition parameters, we find a preferred transition density of \(n_\mathrm{t}\sim2.7\text{--}2.8\,n_0\), a sizable energy-density jump of \(600\text{--}700\) MeV, and a relatively large post-transition sound speed of \(c_s^2/c^2\sim0.85\). Such a phase transition generates a disconnected hybrid branch with radii of about \(6\text{--}7\) km at masses around \(1.2\text{--}1.4\,M_\odot\), and strongly suppresses the dimensionless tidal deformability relative to the purely hadronic branch. This pronounced change in tidal deformability is a characteristic signature of the twin-star mechanism and may provide an important observational tool for identifying phase transitions in neutron-star matter in future multimessenger measurements. These results show that small-radius compact stars can provide direct constraints on both the strength of a first-order phase transition and the stiffness of the post-transition phase in dense matter.

AI.tldr: This paper uses Bayesian methods to model neutron-star EOSs combining NICER data and quark-matter phase transitions, showing that small-radius compact stars can arise from strong first-order phase transitions, producing distinct tidal deformability signatures characteristic of twin stars.
AI.motivation: To investigate the dense-matter EOS in compact stars and test if recent small-radius compact-star candidates can be explained by the twin-star scenario involving a phase transition.
AI.method: A Bayesian framework is utilized, adopting a meta-modeling hadronic EOS constrained by NICER mass-radius data for several pulsars, combined with a constant-speed-of-sound quark-matter EOS segment to model a strong first-order phase transition. Additional observational constraints from small-radius stars are used to fix phase-transition parameters.
AI.result: The analysis favors a phase transition at ~2.7–2.8 times nuclear saturation density with a large energy-density jump and high post-transition sound speed, leading to a disconnected hybrid branch of compact stars with small radii (~6–7 km) and suppressed tidal deformability, consistent with the twin-star mechanism. This highlights the impact of small-radius stars in constraining phase transition properties and EOS stiffness.
AI.conclusion: Small-radius compact stars provide crucial observational evidence supporting strong first-order phase transitions in dense neutron-star matter, enabling constraints on transition density, energy-density jump, and post-transition stiffness, with significant signatures in tidal deformability amenable to multimessenger detection.

title: Cosmological Gravitational Waves from Ultralight Vector Dark Matter
summary: We compute the abundance of cosmological gravitational waves produced during the evolution of an ultralight vector (spin-1) dark matter field. A homogeneous background vector field breaks spatial isotropy, requiring a Bianchi I geometry and inducing a mixing between the scalar, vector, and tensor perturbation sectors. We derive the perturbation equations in this background and show that, as a consequence of this mixing, scalar perturbations act as a source of tensor modes, generating a stochastic GW background. The production and cosmological evolution of these gravitational waves are implemented in a modified version of CLASS, from which we obtain the present-day spectrum.

AI.tldr: The paper computes the gravitational wave background produced by an ultralight vector dark matter field breaking isotropy, showing that scalar perturbations source tensor modes yielding a stochastic GW background, and calculates the present-day spectrum using modified CLASS simulations.
AI.motivation: To study the generation of cosmological gravitational waves sourced by an ultralight vector dark matter field, which breaks spatial isotropy and induces scalar-tensor mode mixing.
AI.method: Derivation of perturbation equations in a Bianchi I geometry background sourced by a homogeneous ultralight vector field, accounting for scalar-vector-tensor mixing; numerical implementation of gravitational wave production and evolution using a modified CLASS code.
AI.result: A stochastic gravitational wave background is generated by scalar perturbations acting as sources for tensor modes due to mode mixing induced by the vector dark matter; present-day gravitational wave spectrum is computed.
AI.conclusion: Ultralight vector dark matter fields can source cosmological gravitational waves through scalar-to-tensor mode coupling in anisotropic backgrounds, resulting in a detectable stochastic gravitational wave background today.

title: Impact of the Infrared Cutoff on Structure Formation in Tsallis Holographic Dark Energy
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures. Comments, especially pointing out missing citations, are welcome
summary: We investigate the viability of Tsallis holographic dark energy (THDE) models, focusing on the role of the infrared (IR) cutoff in the growth of cosmic structures. Considering two commonly used choices of the cutoff, the particle horizon and the future event horizon, we analyze the evolution of linear matter perturbations and compute the growth factor, growth rate, and the observable $fσ_8(z)$. These predictions are compared with observational data from redshift-space distortion measurements. We find that the growth history is highly sensitive to the choice of IR cutoff. Models based on the future event horizon are consistent with observational data and can provide a fit comparable to, or slightly better than, the $Λ$CDM model for suitable values of the Tsallis parameter $δ$. In contrast, models constructed using the particle horizon generally fail to reproduce the observed growth of structure. These results demonstrate that the viability of THDE models depends crucially on the choice of IR cutoff and highlight the importance of structure formation as a stringent test of generalized holographic dark energy scenarios.

AI.tldr: This study shows that Tsallis holographic dark energy models' ability to match cosmic structure growth strongly depends on the infrared cutoff; models with the future event horizon fit observations well, unlike those with the particle horizon.
AI.motivation: To evaluate the viability of Tsallis holographic dark energy (THDE) models in explaining cosmic structure growth and to understand the impact of the infrared (IR) cutoff choice on these models.
AI.method: Analyzing the evolution of linear matter perturbations and calculating growth factor, growth rate, and the observable fσ8(z) for THDE models using two IR cutoffs—the particle horizon and future event horizon—then comparing predictions with observational redshift-space distortion data.
AI.result: THDE models with the future event horizon as the IR cutoff align well with observational data and potentially outperform the ΛCDM model for certain Tsallis parameter values, while models using the particle horizon fail to match observed structure growth.
AI.conclusion: The success of THDE models critically depends on the IR cutoff choice, with the future event horizon offering a viable and observationally consistent framework, underscoring structure formation as a key test for generalized holographic dark energy models.

title: Energy Loss of Newborn Magnetars by Schwinger Process
summary: We investigate electron--positron pair creation through the Schwinger process in newborn magnetars with millisecond spin periods and surface dipole fields close to or above the QED critical field, $B_{\rm Q} = 4.414\times10^{13}\,\mathrm{G}$. In the unscreened field scenario, we derive the analytical global pair creation flux and recast it into a compact form with accurate analytic approximations. For a fiducial model with $B_{\rm p} = 10^{14}\,\mathrm{G}$ and $P_0 = 1\,\mathrm{ms}$, the Schwinger channel exceeds the classical Goldreich--Julian particle supply by many orders of magnitude and becomes the dominant source of charges at the earliest stage of the magnetar. The associated discharge removes about $90\%$ of the initial rotational energy within 30 ms, suppresses the gravitational-wave loss channel, and implies that the observable millisecond phase is extremely short in this unscreened scenario. The rapid energy release over such a short timescale may also provide a viable power source for astrophysical transients. Extending the same fiducial model to $10^4\,\mathrm{yr}$ gives spin periods of order seconds, linking newborn millisecond magnetars to the mature magnetar population.

AI.tldr: The Schwinger process enables prolific electron-positron pair creation in newborn millisecond magnetars, powering rapid energy dissipation that shapes their early spin evolution and transient emission.
AI.motivation: To understand the efficiency and energetic impact of the Schwinger pair creation mechanism on the early evolution of newborn millisecond magnetars and their observable properties.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of global electron-positron pair creation flux via the Schwinger process in magnetar magnetic fields near or exceeding the QED critical field, using accurate analytic approximations.
AI.result: The Schwinger pair creation rate greatly surpasses classical Goldreich-Julian particle supply, dominates charge production initially, rapidly dissipates rotational energy (about 90% in 30 ms), suppresses gravitational-wave emission, and drastically shortens the millisecond observable phase in unscreened magnetic fields.
AI.conclusion: Newborn magnetars with ultra-strong unscreened fields experience fast Schwinger-induced discharge, linking their initial millisecond rotation to longer spin periods over 10^4 years, explaining the transition to mature magnetars and providing a possible power source for short astrophysical transients.

title: Cosmological discrete self-similarity in primordial black hole formation
summary: We demonstrate that discrete self-similarity (DSS), originally discovered in the collapse of a massless scalar field in an asymptotically flat system, survives in primordial black hole (PBH) formation within an expanding cosmological background. Using fully relativistic numerical simulations of massless scalar-field collapse in an Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker universe, we resolve the critical regime down to $|p-p_c|\sim 10^{-8}$, where $p$ and $p_c$ respectively are a parameter of the family of initial data and its threshold value, and find clear log-periodic oscillations in the PBH mass scaling relation. The detailed structure of these oscillations differs from that previously reported in the asymptotically flat case, exhibiting a more pronounced asymmetry between peaks and troughs. Analyzing two distinct families of initial data (Gaussian and piecewise rational curvature profiles), we find critical exponents and DSS periods that differ slightly but are broadly consistent within uncertainties. The presence of DSS implies characteristic log-periodic modulations in the PBH mass spectrum, with potential consequences for PBH abundances and the spectrum of induced gravitational waves.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that discrete self-similarity exists in primordial black hole formation in expanding universes, producing log-periodic mass oscillations with distinct features from flat spacetime cases, confirmed by detailed numerical simulations.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether discrete self-similarity (DSS), known from scalar field collapse in asymptotically flat spacetime, persists in primordial black hole formation in an expanding cosmological background.
AI.method: Using fully relativistic numerical simulations of massless scalar-field collapse in a Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker universe, the authors examined critical phenomena near the threshold of black hole formation for different initial data profiles, resolving the behavior close to criticality.
AI.result: Clear log-periodic oscillations in the primordial black hole (PBH) mass scaling relation were found, with differences in the oscillation structure compared to the asymptotically flat case, including a more pronounced asymmetry between peaks and troughs. Critical exponents and DSS periods vary slightly between initial data families but remain consistent within uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: Discrete self-similarity survives in PBH formation within an expanding cosmological background, implying characteristic log-periodic modulations in the PBH mass spectrum, which may impact PBH abundances and the induced gravitational wave spectrum.

title: Aspects of gravitational clustering and structure formation in the Universe
summary: The distribution of galaxies, halo abundance, and peculiar velocities are influenced by non-linear gravitational interactions, making the study of non-linear evolution crucial for accurate cosmological predictions. We explore these aspects using N-body simulations. Theoretical models of the halo mass function (HMF) can be formulated without referencing a cosmological model or input power spectrum. HMF obtained from N-body simulations show systematic deviations of 5-20\% from theoretical predictions. The physical origin of deviations may result from cosmology, the power spectrum, or both. We examine HMF deviations from universality for scale-free power spectra with an Einstein-de Sitter cosmology. We demonstrate that the mass function exhibits an explicit dependence on the slope of the input power spectrum. We find that an effective index of the $Λ$CDM model can correspond to the HMF from scale-free cosmologies as a first approximation. Furthermore, structure formation has led to deviations from homogeneity and isotropy on scales up to at least $100$ Mpc/h, expected to affect measurements of $H_0$. We revisit this issue of the concordance model. We find a correlation between errors in $H_0$ estimates and the density around the observer. Further, our mock observations reveal that deviations of up to 5\% can occur in Milky Way-sized halos. While this finding alone does not fully resolve the Hubble tension, it may account for part of it. It is essential to understand the limitations of N-body simulations to avoid misinterpreting data. We show that the missing power at small scales introduces errors in the root-mean-square fluctuations and in the simulated mass function. Our analytical calculation indicates that mode coupling between small and large scales depends on resolving collapsed halos. Therefore, accurate mode coupling estimates require sufficient halos in the simulation.

AI.tldr: This work uses N-body simulations to study non-linear gravitational effects on halo mass functions and local Hubble constant measurements, revealing dependencies on power spectrum slope and environment, and stresses the need to resolve small-scale structures for accurate cosmological inferences.
AI.motivation: Precise cosmological predictions require understanding non-linear gravitational effects influencing galaxy and halo distributions and local velocity fields. Discrepancies in halo mass function predictions and local H0 measurements motivate re-examination of simulation limits and the role of power spectrum and environmental factors to improve model accuracy and address tensions in cosmology.
AI.method: The authors employ N-body simulations to measure halo mass functions and analyze peculiar velocities, comparing these to theoretical halo mass function models without prior cosmological assumptions. They use scale-free power spectra within an Einstein-de Sitter framework to isolate effects and simulate mock observations for local H0 estimates. Analytical calculations assess the impact of missing small-scale power and mode coupling on simulation accuracy.
AI.result: The paper investigates non-linear gravitational effects on galaxy distribution, halo abundance, and peculiar velocities using N-body simulations. It focuses on deviations in the halo mass function (HMF) from theoretical models, showing these depend on the power spectrum slope and cosmology. The study highlights scale-free cosmologies with Einstein-de Sitter backgrounds to understand deviations and relates these to ΛCDM models. It also examines how large-scale structure influences local measurements of the Hubble constant (H0), finding environmental density correlations that may partially explain observed H0 tensions. Additionally, it addresses limitations in N-body simulations, notably missing small-scale power affecting fluctuations and mass function accuracy, emphasizing the need for sufficient halo resolution to capture mode coupling effects.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that the halo mass function deviates systematically from universal theoretical predictions due to cosmology and power spectrum dependence. Environmental density can influence local H0 measurements causing deviations up to 5%. Limitations in N-body simulations, particularly missing small-scale power, induce errors that must be accounted for by ensuring sufficient halo resolution to correctly model mode coupling.

title: Impact of Primordial Black Hole population on 21 cm observables at high redshift
summary: The 21-cm signal, one of the most promising probes of the high-redshift Universe, has traditionally been modelled without accounting for the effects of active galactic nuclei (AGN) in the pre-JWST era, primarily due to the lack of observational evidence for AGNs at z > 6. However, following the discovery of several AGNs at redshifts as high as z ~ 10 by JWST, it has become imperative to incorporate the impact of these early AGNs when predicting the 21-cm signal. Supposing that these AGNs are seeded by primordial black holes (PBHs), we study their impact with a semi-numerical model setup. Specifically, we extended the explicitly photon-conserving reionization framework, SCRIPT, including essential cosmic dawn physics and PBH contributions. This enables us to compute both the global signal and the power spectrum of the 21-cm line over the redshift range z ~ 30 - 5 within a self-consistent framework. Building on this setup, we then investigate the impact of different PBH mass functions (obeying current observational constraints) on the resulting signal. The X-ray heating from PBHs can substantially make the depth of the global 21-cm signal shallower and suppress the expected power amplitude during cosmic dawn. We also find that the choice of mass function plays a crucial role in shaping the 21-cm signal, and can, in fact, lead to significantly different predictions.

AI.tldr: Incorporating primordial black hole-seeded AGNs, newly discovered at high redshifts by JWST, into a self-consistent semi-numerical model shows significant alterations to the cosmic dawn 21-cm signal, with X-ray heating effects reducing signal depth and power amplitude. The PBH mass function critically shapes these outcomes.
AI.motivation: Recent JWST discoveries of AGNs at redshifts up to z ~ 10 necessitate incorporating their impact on the 21-cm signal, which was previously modeled without AGNs due to lack of observational evidence beyond z > 6. Considering PBHs as seeds for these early AGNs, the study aims to understand their influence on the 21-cm cosmological signal.
AI.method: We employed a semi-numerical modeling approach by extending the photon-conserving reionization framework SCRIPT to include cosmic dawn physics and primordial black hole (PBH) contributions, allowing self-consistent computation of both the global 21-cm signal and its power spectrum from redshift z ~ 30 to 5.
AI.result: The inclusion of PBH-driven AGNs significantly affects the 21-cm signal by shallowing the global signal depth and suppressing the power spectrum amplitude during cosmic dawn due to X-ray heating. Furthermore, different PBH mass functions drastically alter the signal predictions, emphasizing the importance of mass function choice under existing observational constraints.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for early AGNs seeded by primordial black holes is crucial for accurate modeling of the 21-cm signal across high redshifts, as their X-ray heating impacts signal observables significantly, and varying the PBH mass function leads to notably different predictions, influencing future observations and theoretical frameworks.

title: Multi-wavelength study of EP250416a / GRB 250416C: An Optically Dark Long GRB with a Late Jet Break
comment: 12 pages, 14 figures, 4 tables, submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: We present multi-wavelength study of the $γ$/X-ray transient EP250416a (also designated GRB 250416C), triggered by the Einstein Probe (EP) Wide-field X-ray Telescope and also by SVOM and Konus-Wind. Observations spanning the gamma-ray, X-ray, and optical bands facilitated detailed analysis of the burst's prompt emission, afterglow evolution, and physical origin. EP250416a exhibits a burst duration of 30 s in X-ray and 17.7 s in gamma-rays, with joint spectral fitting of 0.5-5000 keV data gives $E\rm_{peak}=342_{-232}^{+90}$ keV. Optical spectroscopy of the afterglow, acquired with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) on Gemini South, yielded a redshift of $z=0.963$. Accounting for the measured redshift, the isotropic energies are $E\rm_{X,iso}=2.7_{-0.5}^{+0.9}\times10^{50}$ erg and $E\rm_{γ,iso}=7.34_{-2.1}^{+5.1}\times10^{51}$ erg, aligning with the Amati relation for long GRBs. The fluence ratio $\rm S(25-50~keV)/S(50-100~keV)=0.78_{-0.15}^{+0.1}$ classifies EP250416a as an X-ray rich (XRR) GRB. The X-ray afterglow shows an initial shallow decay ($α\approx -0.5$) transitioning to a canonical decay phase ($α\approx -1$), with a very late jet break at $t\sim 1.5\times 10^6$ s, corresponding to a jet half-opening angle of $θ_j=10.6_{-1.8}^{+1.9}$ degrees. EP250416a is optically dark, as it shows only a faint $r$-band detection ($r=24.16$ mag) from Gemini South-GMOS and a low optical-to-X-ray spectral index $β_{\rm OX} = 0.3$. This may be attributed to significant host-galaxy extinction, with a required $A_V^{\text{host}}=5.5\ \text{mag}$ derived from the extinction curve model.

AI.tldr: This study presents multi-band observations of GRB 250416C, revealing it as a long, X-ray rich GRB with typical afterglow decay, significant host extinction causing optical faintness, and physical parameters consistent with established GRB relations.
AI.motivation: To perform a comprehensive multi-wavelength analysis of the gamma-ray/X-ray transient EP250416a (GRB 250416C) to understand its prompt emission, afterglow evolution, and physical characteristics.
AI.method: Observations across gamma-ray, X-ray, and optical bands were conducted, including spectral fitting from 0.5-5000 keV and optical spectroscopy with Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph to measure redshift and afterglow properties.
AI.result: EP250416a is a long GRB with a burst duration of about 30 s in X-rays and 17.7 s in gamma-rays, with peak energy E_peak around 342 keV. It exhibits isotropic energies consistent with the Amati relation, classifies as an X-ray rich GRB, shows canonical afterglow decay with a jet break indicating a jet opening angle of ~10.6 degrees, and is optically dark suggesting strong host galaxy extinction.
AI.conclusion: EP250416a fits the profile of a long-duration X-ray rich GRB with significant host galaxy extinction accounting for optical darkness, a typical afterglow evolution including a late jet break, and energetic characteristics consistent with known GRB correlations.

title: Saturation Mechanisms in the Interacting Dark Sector
summary: We introduce a family of phenomenological cosmological models featuring an interacting dark sector modulated by a sparseness scale parameter, in order to describe the late-time accelerated expansion of the universe. The sparseness scale, inspired by well-established saturation mechanisms in ecology and biology, is introduced in the interaction as a half-saturation constant that bounds the energy exchange between dark matter and dark energy, controls the dynamical behaviour of the physical variables and can prevent the phantom crossing. We consider three nonlinear interacting models, where two of them recover the linear interacting scenarios when the sparsity parameter vanishes. We examine the phase-space of the cosmological field equations by using the Hubble normalization approach. We determine the stationary points and their stability properties in order to reconstruct the asymptotics behaviour of the field equations. Such an analysis allows us to demonstrate the effects of the sparseness scale on the background dynamics. We test the interacting models with observational data. Specifically, we employ Supernovae catalogues, cosmic chronometers, Baryon Acoustic Oscillation measurements from DESI DR2, and redshift-space distortion measurements of the growth of large-scale structure through the $f$ and $fσ_8$ observables. The Bayesian analysis suggests that, for two of the three models, a vanishing sparsity parameter is disfavoured at more than the 95\% confidence interval, providing observational support for a nonzero sparseness scale in the dark sector interaction.

AI.tldr: This study introduces and analyzes dark sector interaction models with a sparseness scale parameter, demonstrating its theoretical effects on cosmic evolution and confirming its necessity via observational data analysis.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to better model the late-time accelerated expansion of the universe by introducing a physically inspired sparseness scale parameter to regulate dark matter-dark energy interactions, controlling energy exchange and dynamics, and preventing problematic phantom crossing behavior.
AI.method: The authors construct nonlinear interacting dark sector models modulated by a sparseness scale parameter acting as a half-saturation constant. They perform phase-space dynamical analysis using Hubble normalization, identify stationary points, and assess their stability to understand asymptotic behaviors. Observational constraints are obtained through Bayesian analysis using Supernovae catalogs, cosmic chronometers, BAO from DESI DR2, and redshift-space distortion growth measurements.
AI.result: This paper proposes novel phenomenological cosmological models incorporating a sparseness scale parameter to modulate interactions between dark matter and dark energy, aiming to explain late-time accelerated expansion. The sparseness scale acts as a half-saturation constant limiting energy exchange, influencing dynamics and preventing phantom crossing. Three nonlinear interaction models are studied, two reducing to linear interactions when the parameter vanishes. Dynamical system analysis via Hubble normalization identifies stable fixed points depicting asymptotic behavior, highlighting the sparseness scale's role in background evolution. Bayesian inference with multiple data sets including Supernovae, cosmic chronometers, BAO from DESI DR2, and growth rate observables shows that two models significantly prefer a nonzero sparseness scale over zero, thus observationally validating the introduced modulation.
AI.conclusion: The inclusion of a sparseness scale in dark sector interactions significantly affects cosmological dynamics and is statistically favored by current observational data in two out of three models, suggesting its relevance for describing late-time cosmic acceleration.

title: Gauging the Impact of Cosmic Ray Feedback on the Stellar Initial Mass Function
comment: 17 Pages, 9 Figures, published in ApJ. arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:2407.17597
summary: Cosmic rays (CRs) drive ionization and influence gas dynamics in molecular clouds (MCs), potentially impacting the resulting star formation outcomes. Although previous simulations of individual star formation have included methods for cosmic ray transport (CRT), none have been large enough to resolve the stellar initial mass function (IMF). We conduct numerical simulations following the collapse of a $20000 M_{\odot}$ MC and the subsequent star formation including CRT, both with and without CRs accelerated by winds from the young massive stars, and compare against a non-CRT simulation. We show that after the first massive stars form, the cavity produced by feedback is more pronounced in the CRT simulations because the external CRs are able to propagate inwards and compress the gas into higher density structures. This increases the subsequent star formation in the cloud; by the end of the simulation, the SFE in the CRT simulation including stellar wind CRs is 43 \% higher than the non-CRT simulation. The IMF is also top heavy in comparison, with a slope above 1 $M_{\odot}$ that is shallower by $\sim 20$ \%. These effects are also present in the simulation without wind-accelerated CRs, but they are not as pronounced; the SFE is only 16 \% higher than the non-CRT simulation, and the IMF high-mass slope is shallower by $\sim 10$ \%. These results may explain some of the observed top-heavy IMFs, which typically occur in high-CR environments such as the galactic center.

AI.tldr: Cosmic ray transport in molecular clouds boosts star formation efficiency and leads to a top-heavy initial mass function, especially when including cosmic rays from stellar winds.
AI.motivation: To investigate how cosmic rays influence ionization, gas dynamics, and ultimately star formation efficiency (SFE) and the initial mass function (IMF) in molecular clouds, resolving the IMF in a large enough simulation.
AI.method: Numerical simulations of molecular cloud collapse and star formation including cosmic ray transport (CRT), comparing cases with CRT (with and without CRs from stellar winds) and without CRT.
AI.result: Simulations show CRT leads to more pronounced feedback cavities as CRs propagate and compress gas, enhancing star formation. Including stellar wind CRs increases SFE by 43% and makes the IMF top-heavy with a 20% shallower slope above 1 solar mass. Without wind CRs, SFE increases by 16% and the IMF slope is shallower by 10%.
AI.conclusion: Cosmic rays, particularly those accelerated by young massive stars, significantly impact star formation by compressing gas into denser regions, increasing star formation efficiency and shifting the IMF to be top-heavy, potentially explaining observed top-heavy IMFs in high cosmic ray environments.

title: Magnetar Engines in Broad-lined Type Ic Supernovae and a Unified Picture for Magnetar-powered Stripped-envelope Supernovae
comment: 39 pages, 17 figures, 3 tables, Comments are welcome!
summary: We model the multi-band lightcurves of 80 SNe Ic-BL, including 11 associated with lGRBs, using a magnetar engine model with $^{56}$Ni decay. We find that the data are all consistent with a magnetar central engine, and such a model yields high-quality fits across the sample. The medians with $1σ$ regions of the key parameters are $P_{\rm{i}}\sim2.04^{+1.84}_{-0.96}\,{\rm{ms}}$, $B_{\rm{p}}\sim3.96^{+3.28}_{-1.40}\times10^{15}\,{\rm{G}}$, $M_{\rm{ej}}\sim2.30^{+1.48}_{-1.02}\,M_\odot$, and $M_{\rm{Ni}}\sim0.18^{+0.14}_{-0.09}\,M_\odot$, with strong and statistically significant correlations observed for both $M_{\rm{ej}}-P_{\rm{i}}$ (anti-correlation) and $M_{\rm{Ni}}-M_{\rm{ej}}$ (correlation). Comparing the SN Ic-BL samples with and without lGRB association using fitting parameters, we find no significant difference between them, although the GRB-associated sample is slightly brighter, possibly due to an observational bias. Relative to ordinary SNe Ic, SNe Ic-BL have similar $^{56}$Ni and ejecta masses, suggesting comparable pre-SN progenitor properties, with differences possibly arising from the presence of a magnetar engine. In comparison with other possible magnetar-powered SESNe, including SLSNe Ic and FBOTs, we confirm a strong universal $M_{\rm{ej}}-P_{\rm{i}}$ correlation, indicating a common origin. SNe Ic-BL and SLSNe Ic have similar ejecta mass distributions, typically $M_{\rm ej}\gtrsim0.5\,M_\odot$, while FBOTs mostly lie below this value. Differences between SNe Ic-BL and SLSNe Ic may arise from magnetar properties, with SN Ic-BL magnetars rotating faster and having stronger fields. Moreover, the $P_{\rm{i}}-B_{\rm{p}}$ distribution of lGRB magnetars largely overlaps with that of SN Ic-BL magnetars. In connection with binary simulation results, we propose a unified physical classification and progenitor framework for magnetar-powered and ordinary SESNe.

AI.tldr: This study models 80 SNe Ic-BL lightcurves with a magnetar plus $^{56}$Ni decay model, finding consistent magnetar engine properties across samples, no clear difference with or without lGRBs, and a universal ejecta mass–spin period relation linking them with other supernova types, supporting a unified magnetar-driven progenitor framework.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical origins and engine properties of broad-lined Type Ic supernovae (SNe Ic-BL), including those associated with long gamma-ray bursts (lGRBs), and to explore the role of magnetar engines and $^{56}$Ni decay in powering their lightcurves.
AI.method: Model multi-band lightcurves of 80 SNe Ic-BL (including 11 with lGRBs) using a magnetar central engine model combined with $^{56}$Ni radioactive decay, followed by statistical analysis of key parameters and their correlations, and comparative studies involving other supernova sub-classes and binary simulation results.
AI.result: The magnetar engine model fits all lightcurves well, yielding median initial spin periods (~2 ms), magnetic fields (~4×10^{15} G), ejecta masses (~2.3 M_⊙), and nickel masses (~0.18 M_⊙). Significant anti-correlation between ejecta mass and initial spin period, and correlation between nickel mass and ejecta mass are found. No significant differences exist between lGRB-associated and non-associated SNe Ic-BL in these parameters. SNe Ic-BL share similar $^{56}$Ni and ejecta masses with ordinary SNe Ic but differ in the presumed presence of magnetars. Magnetar properties link SNe Ic-BL, superluminous SNe Ic (SLSNe Ic), and fast blue optical transients (FBOTs) via a universal ejecta mass–spin period correlation. Differences among these arise from variations in magnetar spin and magnetic field strengths. The spin-field distributions of magnetars associated with lGRBs and SNe Ic-BL overlap substantially, supporting a unified progenitor framework.
AI.conclusion: Magnetar engines effectively power SNe Ic-BL and connect them physically to lGRBs and other supernova subtypes, endorsing a unified model of progenitors influenced by spin, magnetic field, and binary evolution.

title: An RXTE Search for the Sterile Neutrino Decay in Galaxy Clusters
summary: We have searched for the 3.55 keV line from sterile neutrino decay using 3.1 megaseconds of RXTE cluster data. A 2.5$σ$ excess of emission over a thermal model is found over the energy span of the 3.55 keV line in the combined spectra of the eight clusters that individually have an excess. The residuals are added to increase the signal to noise ratio of the excess, which is then modeled with a Gaussian to simulate the instrumental spectral response. We find a significant correlation (r = 0.76) for a line centered at 3.6 keV with a model flux of 3.07 x 10$^{-5}$ ph cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. Mixing angle for detected clusters ranges from 0.35 to 6.2 x 10$^{-10}$. The decay rate inferred from the line flux is strongly correlated (r = 0.87) with cluster temperature, which is due to hotter, more massive clusters having a larger amount of dark matter. Approximately half of the decay line total flux comes from the Coma cluster. We fit the Coma cluster spectrum with two different three-component models. The first includes a Gaussian fixed at 3.55 keV to model soft emission. The second three-component model uses a second thermal component to model soft emission. The model fit parameters indicate that the second thermal component is modeling high-energy residuals rather than low ones, where the Gaussian is. Though our line fluxes exceed most reported detections and upper limits, they do not overproduce the dark matter. We conclude that some fraction of the marginally detected excess could be attributed to the decay line since low-temperature thermal emission and systematics fail to model it completely.

AI.tldr: The study reports a marginal 2.5 sigma detection of the 3.55 keV line from sterile neutrino decay in galaxy clusters using RXTE data, with line flux correlating with cluster temperature and dark matter amount, supporting the possibility that sterile neutrino decay contributes to the observed excess.
AI.motivation: To search for evidence of the 3.55 keV emission line associated with sterile neutrino decay in galaxy clusters, which would provide insights into dark matter properties.
AI.method: Combined spectral analysis of eight galaxy clusters using RXTE data, Gaussian modeling of residuals to simulate instrumental response, correlation analyses of flux and cluster properties, and comparative spectral modeling of the Coma cluster using multi-component models.
AI.result: Detected a 2.5 sigma excess emission at ~3.6 keV in combined cluster spectra; significant correlation of line flux with cluster temperature (r = 0.87) and dark matter content; mixing angles ranging from 0.35 to 6.2 x 10^-10; approximately half of the total decay line flux originates from the Coma cluster; line fluxes higher than most reported detections but consistent with dark matter constraints.
AI.conclusion: Some fraction of the marginal excess emission detected in the data can be attributed to the 3.55 keV decay line from sterile neutrinos, as thermal emission and systematic uncertainties alone cannot fully explain the observed excess.

title: Mitigating Systematic Errors in Parameter Estimation of Binary Black Hole Mergers in O1-O3 LIGO-Virgo Data
comment: 23 pages, 13 figures, 2 tables. Comments are welcome
summary: Systematic errors in the parameter estimation (PE) of gravitational wave (GW) mergers can arise from various sources, including waveform systematics, noise mischaracterization, data analysis artifacts, and other unknown factors. In this study, we analyze selected events from the first three observing runs of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) collaboration. We choose events that have been flagged in various studies as potentially affected by systematic errors. Here, we reanalyze these events using a couple of parametric models developed in previous work that incorporate uncertainties in both the phase and amplitude of the GW waveform. In this data-driven approach, we apply sufficiently broad priors on the uncertainty parameters to account for potential systematic errors. Our findings show that the proposed method effectively reduces systematic errors, even those arising from data artifacts, such as glitches occurring near a signal and the deglitching process in GW frame files. Similarly, inconsistent results from different waveform models become much more consistent in our framework. One noteworthy event we examine is GW191109\_010717, which is particularly interesting due to its anti-aligned spin properties. We report that, within our framework, the event still exhibits anti-aligned spin characteristics, but the inference results become consistent across raw and deglitched frame files, as well as across the waveform models used for this event (IMRPhenomXPHM, IMRPhenomXO4a, and NRSur7dq4). A similar trend is observed for the event GW200129\_065458, which previously yielded a high, but inconsistent precession parameter among different waveform models. In contrast, we observe a non-zero and consistent value of $χ_{p}=0.60^{+0.31}_{-0.33}, 0.58^{+0.30}_{-0.29}$ and $0.56^{+0.31}_{-0.28}$ for the IMRPhenomXPHM, IMRPhenomXO4a, and NRSur7dq4 waveform models, respectively.

AI.tldr: This study introduces a parametric model-based approach to mitigate systematic errors in gravitational wave parameter estimation, achieving more consistent results across waveform models and data artifacts for several LVK events, notably GW191109_010717 and GW200129_065458.
AI.motivation: To address and mitigate systematic errors in gravitational wave parameter estimation arising from waveform uncertainties, noise, and data artifacts, which affect the reliability of astrophysical inferences.
AI.method: Reanalysis of selected LVK gravitational wave events using parametric models that incorporate broad uncertainty priors in both phase and amplitude to account for systematic errors.
AI.result: The framework reduces systematic errors, harmonizes results across different waveform models and data conditions, and provides consistent and reliable parameter estimates for events such as GW191109_010717 and GW200129_065458, including spin and precession parameters.
AI.conclusion: The data-driven parametric framework effectively reduces systematic errors in gravitational wave parameter estimation and reconciles inconsistencies across waveform models and data artifacts.

title: Testing solitonic boson star interpretations of Sagittarius A* with near-infrared flare astrometry
summary: We use GRAVITY near-infrared (NIR) flare astrometry to test whether Sagittarius A* could be a solitonic boson star. We consider five spherically symmetric solitonic boson-star models with different effective radii, together with the Schwarzschild black hole. Treating the flares as hot spots on circular equatorial orbits, we analyze their centroid motions and images in these spacetimes and use them for parameter fitting. We perform the fitting using both $χ^2$ analysis and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, which yield consistent results: the inferred masses of boson-star models are systematically larger than the established value of $4.3\times10^6M_\odot$. Notably, more diffusive boson stars exhibit imaging properties closer to those of a black hole, leading to mass estimates that are correspondingly closer to the established value. Overall, our results place stringent constraints on solitonic boson star interpretations of Sagittarius A*, although do not completely rule them out.

AI.tldr: Using GRAVITY NIR astrometry, the paper tests solitonic boson star models for Sagittarius A*, finding that these models imply larger masses than the known mass of 4.3 million solar masses and are less compatible with observed flare properties than a black hole, though not entirely ruled out.
AI.motivation: To investigate if Sagittarius A*, traditionally interpreted as a black hole, could instead be a solitonic boson star by comparing astrometric observations of NIR flares with predictions from boson star and black hole models.
AI.method: The paper models flares as hot spots on circular equatorial orbits around Sagittarius A* and analyzes their centroid motions and images in both boson star and Schwarzschild black hole spacetimes. Parameter fitting is performed using chi-square analysis and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods to infer mass and other model parameters.
AI.result: The study uses near-infrared flare astrometry from the GRAVITY instrument to test whether Sagittarius A* can be explained as a solitonic boson star instead of a black hole. Five spherically symmetric solitonic boson star models with varying effective radii are compared against the standard Schwarzschild black hole model. The analysis treats flares as hot spots on circular equatorial orbits and analyzes their centroid motions and images for parameter inference. Both χ² and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods are employed for fitting. The findings indicate that boson star models infer systematically higher masses than the established mass of Sagittarius A*. More diffusive boson stars produce imaging features closer to the black hole, yielding mass estimates nearer to the accepted value. The study places strong constraints on the viability of solitonic boson stars as Sagittarius A* but does not fully exclude them.
AI.conclusion: The solitonic boson star interpretation of Sagittarius A* is strongly constrained by the GRAVITY NIR flare astrometry, with models yielding systematically higher mass estimates than the well-established black hole mass. While more diffusive boson stars mimic black hole imaging properties better, the overall data do not fully support a boson star scenario but also do not definitively exclude it.
